content: The Global Dementia Observatory (GDO) Reference Guide, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2018, provides detailed guidance on the use, adaptation, and redistribution of its content for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. The WHO logo cannot be used, and any adaptations of the work must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not produced by WHO and that WHO is not responsible for its content or accuracy. The original English version remains the authoritative edition. Disputes arising under the license are to be mediated according to the rules of the World Intellectual Property Organization. The guide emphasizes that any reuse of third-party materials, such as tables, figures, or images, requires the user to determine and obtain permission from the copyright holder. WHO is not liable for claims resulting from the infringement of third-party-owned components. The designations and presentation of materials in the publication do not imply any opinion on the legal status of countries, territories, or boundaries. WHO does not endorse specific organizations, products, or services mentioned in the publication. Dementia is described as a progressive condition affecting memory, cognitive abilities, and behavior, significantly impairing daily living activities. Alzheimer’s disease is the most common form, accounting for 60–70% of cases, followed by vascular dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies, and frontotemporal dementia. Mixed forms of dementia often coexist. Globally, approximately 50 million people are affected by dementia, with this number projected to rise to 82 million by 2030 and 152 million by 2050. Nearly 60% of individuals with dementia live in lowand middle-income countries, where most new cases are expected to occur. Dementia is the seventh leading cause of death worldwide and a major contributor to disability and dependency among older adults, impacting not only individuals but also their caregivers, families, and communities. In 2012, WHO launched the report Dementia: A Public Health Priority in collaboration with Alzheimer’s Disease International to raise awareness and advocate for action at international and national levels. This was followed by the First Ministerial Conference on Global Action Against Dementia in 2015, which emphasized the importance of promoting and monitoring global and national efforts on dementia. The Global Dementia Observatory (GDO) was established to collect and disseminate data on key dementia indicators, supporting countries in addressing the needs of individuals with dementia and their caregivers. The GDO aims to strengthen policies, support evidence-based service planning, and build capacity across health and social care systems. In 2017, the Seventieth World Health Assembly adopted the Global Action Plan on the Public Health Response to Dementia 2017–2025, outlining clear actions for Member States, the WHO Secretariat, and partners, along with global targets and indicators for tracking progress. The GDO serves as the monitoring mechanism for this action plan, providing data to measure progress toward achieving global targets. The GDO framework consists of three domains—Policy, Service Delivery, and Information & Research—each with multiple subdomains and seven strategic themes. These themes align with the action areas of the global action plan and serve as national goals for introducing, improving, or monitoring dementia-related activities. Indicators within the framework are used to collect key information on dementia and monitor relevant actions at the national level. Specific indicators measure individual countries’ contributions toward achieving global targets. The GDO e-tool, available in English, French, and Spanish, facilitates data collection through a structured online survey. It allows users to enter, save, and resume data entry, with automatic skipping of irrelevant subquestions. Data is finalized and uploaded to WHO upon confirmation. The person submitting the data must have the authority to do so and agree to the terms for data provision to WHO.
